title: Joy opens the heart
hook: Hasidism treats joy as a spiritual force, sadness as a closing

segments.voice: Yesterday, devekut, holding on to God through the whole day, even in the middle of a chore. Your line was cling. Which chore did you pick, and did the holding last? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-two.

A hand that is clenched can't receive anything. Try it right now if you like: make a fist, and then try to take a cup from someone. You can't. You have to open first. Yesterday's word asked how a person holds on to God all day long. Underneath it sits another question: what keeps a person from holding on? Hasidic teaching points somewhere you might not look first. Sadness. Heaviness. The gray mood that closes the hand. And the thing that opens it again is today's word.
screen: `A CLENCHED HAND CAN'T RECEIVE.` → `WHAT CLOSES IT?` → `HEAVINESS.`

segments.voice: Simcha. Joy, gladness, the word wedding guests use when they wish a family more simchas. First, the verse. The psalm says, "Serve the LORD with gladness; come before His presence with singing." Notice that gladness isn't the reward at the end of the service. It is the way the service is done. Second, the Talmud. In tractate Shabbat the sages teach that the Divine Presence does not rest on a person in the middle of sadness or laziness, but in the middle of the joy of a mitzvah. Read that way, a mood can be a door, or a wall. Third, the Hasidic turn. The early Hasidic teachers took that teaching and made it central. Joy, for them, isn't a feeling you wait for. It's a force, something that opens the heart so prayer can go up and blessing can come down. Sadness, in their language, is a closing, a contraction, and they treated it as something to work against, not something to admire. Fourth, and this matters: they didn't mean pretending. Hasidic teachers made a careful distinction. A broken heart, honest sorrow over a wrong you did, they valued. That kind of sorrow moves you. What they warned against was the heavy, stuck sadness that only sits there and closes everything. One is a door being knocked on. The other is a door locked from inside. So simcha isn't the absence of pain. It's the hand staying open, even in a hard week.
screen: `SERVE WITH GLADNESS.` · `A MOOD CAN BE A DOOR OR A WALL.` · `JOY AS A FORCE THAT OPENS.` · `A BROKEN HEART IS NOT A CLOSED ONE.` · then, large: `JOY OPENS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one joy. Settle, and let your hands rest open in your lap, palms up. Breathe. Now look for one thing in your life right now that is good. It doesn't need to be big. Warm socks. A message from a friend. The fact that your coffee is still hot. When you find it, stay with it. Don't explain it away, don't add a but. Just let it be good for a minute, and notice whether anything in your chest loosens. If you pray, you can say the psalm's words, serve the LORD with gladness, and let them sit. The bell holds the time.
Simcha. Joy, gladness. For the Hasidic teachers, a spiritual force that opens the heart, where heavy sadness closes it. Today's word.
Your line: joy opens. Today, when you feel yourself clench, unclench one hand on purpose and look for one small good thing in the room. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: In Hasidic communities joy is cultivated on purpose: singing wordless melodies called niggunim, dancing at weddings and festivals, and teaching that a mitzvah done gladly is done fully.

pairs: the Presence rests in the joy of a mitzvah

myth: Hasidic teachers said all sorrow is bad
they valued a broken heart over a real wrong. what they warned against was heavy, stuck sadness.
in the psalm, gladness is the way the service is done
"serve the LORD with gladness": joy isn't the prize at the end, it's the manner.
simcha means pretending to be happy
the teachers meant an open heart, not a mask over pain.

fork.setup: you're in a gray, heavy week. a Hasidic teacher would say the first thing to work on is:
options: the heaviness itself, because it closes the heart.
nothing, wait until the mood passes.
fork.reveal: they treated stuck sadness as a closing, something to work against, because joy is what opens the heart to prayer.

original.note: Hebrew: joy, gladness. Also the everyday word for a happy family occasion.

trapdoor: what you thought: being in a good mood.
what it means: gladness as the way of serving God, an open heart where heavy sadness closes it.
what a scholar hears: the Talmud's teaching that the Divine Presence rests in the joy of a mitzvah, taken up by Hasidism and made central to its life of prayer.

sources.quoted: Serve the LORD with gladness; come before His presence with singing.

notes: Psalm 100:2 quoted from JPS 1917; please confirm exact wording and punctuation.
Shabbat 30b paraphrased (the Shechinah rests not amid sadness or laziness but amid the joy of a mitzvah).

The Hasidic distinction between a broken heart (lev nishbar) and heavy sadness (atzvut) is stated generally without naming a source; a Keeper may want to anchor it in Tanya ch. 26 or 31, or in Breslov teaching.
